claim: BK channels regulate calcium-dependent cellular events such as neurotransmitter release by limiting calcium influx.
source: Voltage- and calcium-dependent BK channels regulate calcium-dependent cellular events such as neurotransmitter release by limiting calcium influx.
evidence: This is a well-established function of BK channels supported by scientific consensus and citations in the introduction.

claim: ERG-28 is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein.
source: In C. elegans, we show that ERG-28, an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein, promotes the trafficking of SLO-1 BK channels from the ER to the plasma membrane by shielding them from premature degradation.
evidence: Supported by localization data showing ERG-28 co-localizes with ER markers (Figure 3C, 3F) and has ER retention motif.

claim: ERG-28 promotes the trafficking of SLO-1 BK channels from the ER to the plasma membrane.
source: In C. elegans, we show that ERG-28, an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein, promotes the trafficking of SLO-1 BK channels from the ER to the plasma membrane by shielding them from premature degradation.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced SLO-1 at plasma membrane in erg-28 mutants (Figure 4A) and restoration by ERG-28 expression (Figure 4B, C).

claim: In the absence of ERG-28, SLO-1 channels undergo aspartic protease DDI-1-dependent degradation.
source: In the absence of ERG-28, SLO-1 channels undergo aspartic protease DDI-1-dependent degradation, resulting in markedly reduced expression at presynaptic terminals.
evidence: Supported by data showing ddi-1 mutation partially restores SLO-1 expression in erg-28 mutants (Figure 5B-D).

claim: Loss of erg-28 results in markedly reduced SLO-1 expression at presynaptic terminals.
source: In the absence of ERG-28, SLO-1 channels undergo aspartic protease DDI-1-dependent degradation, resulting in markedly reduced expression at presynaptic terminals.
evidence: Directly shown in Figure 4A comparing wild-type and erg-28 mutants.

claim: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in locomotion.
source: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in locomotion, neurotransmitter release, and calcium-mediated asymmetric differentiation of the AWC olfactory neuron pair
evidence: Demonstrated by speed measurements showing erg-28 mutation improves sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf) (Figure 1A).

claim: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in neurotransmitter release.
source: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in locomotion, neurotransmitter release, and calcium-mediated asymmetric differentiation of the AWC olfactory neuron pair
evidence: Shown by electrophysiology data (Figure 2B-E) and aldicarb sensitivity assays (Figure 2A).

claim: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in calcium-mediated asymmetric differentiation of the AWC olfactory neuron pair.
source: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in locomotion, neurotransmitter release, and calcium-mediated asymmetric differentiation of the AWC olfactory neuron pair
evidence: Demonstrated by str-2 gene expression analysis in AWC neurons (Figure 1D).

claim: Loss of erg-28 conferred significant ethanol-resistant locomotory behavior.
source: Loss of erg-28 suppressed phenotypic defects of slo-1 gain-of-function mutants in locomotion, neurotransmitter release, and calcium-mediated asymmetric differentiation of the AWC olfactory neuron pair, and conferred significant ethanol-resistant locomotory behavior, resembling slo-1 loss-of-function mutants, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: Shown by ethanol-resistant locomotory behavior assays (Figure 6A).

claim: BK channels control presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Hu et al., 2001).
source: BK channels, named for their large K+conductances, control a wide array of calcium-regulated cellular processes, including presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Hu et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2001.

claim: BK channels control action potential firing rate (Gu et al., 2007; Sausbier et al., 2004; Shao et al., 1999).
source: BK channels, named for their large K+conductances, control a wide array of calcium-regulated cellular processes, including presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Hu et al., 2001), action potential firing rate (Gu et al., 2007; Sausbier et al., 2004; Shao et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gu et al., 2007; Sausbier et al., 2004; Shao et al., 1999.

claim: BK channels control muscle excitation (Jaggar et al., 2000).
source: BK channels, named for their large K+conductances, control a wide array of calcium-regulated cellular processes, including presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Hu et al., 2001), action potential firing rate (Gu et al., 2007; Sausbier et al., 2004; Shao et al., 1999), and muscle excitation (Jaggar et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaggar et al., 2000.

claim: Full activation of the BK channel requires coincidental membrane depolarization and elevation in free cytosolic Ca2+ ions (Fakler and Adelman, 2008; Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999).
source: These roles of BK channels result from the unique feature that full activation of the BK channel requires coincidental membrane depolarization and elevation in free cytosolic Ca2+ ions (Fakler and Adelman, 2008; Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fakler and Adelman, 2008; Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999.

claim: BK channel activity is regulated by post-translational modifications, associating auxiliary subunits, its localization at the plasma membrane, and the number of channels expressed at the plasma membrane (Kim and Oh, 2016).
source: BK channel activity is regulated by many factors including post-translational modifications, associating auxiliary subunits, its localization at the plasma membrane, and the number of channels expressed at the plasma membrane (Kim and Oh, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim and Oh, 2016.

claim: Cytoskeletal proteins and cytoskeleton-interacting proteins, including actin, microtubule-associated protein 1A, and filamin A, are reported to alter the level of BK channels at the plasma membrane in vitro (Kim et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2006).
source: For instance, cytoskeletal proteins and cytoskeleton-interacting proteins, including actin, microtubule-associated protein 1A, and filamin A, are reported to alter the level of BK channels at the plasma membrane in vitro (Kim et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2006.

claim: Cereblon mediates the interaction of BK channels with CRL4A E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, which causes ubiquitination of BK channels and their retention in the ER (Liu et al., 2014).
source: A recent study showed that cereblon mediates the interaction of BK channels with CRL4A E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, which causes ubiquitination of BK channels and their retention in the ER (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking BK channel ubiquitination or disrupting the interaction between BK channels and CRL4A E3 ubiquitin ligase increases the surface expression of BK channels in vitro in transfected primary cultured neurons.
source: Blocking BK channel ubiquitination or disrupting the interaction between BK channels and CRL4A E3 ubiquitin ligase was shown to increase the surface expression of BK channels in vitro in transfected primary cultured neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the previous sentence about Liu et al., 2014 study.

claim: BKIP-1, a plasma membrane localized protein, increases the levels of SLO-1 BK channels at the plasma membrane (Chen et al., 2010).
source: In C. elegans, BKIP-1, a plasma membrane localized protein, was shown to increase the levels of SLO-1 BK channels at the plasma membrane (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: The dystrophin complex localizes SLO-1 channels near calcium channels in the sarcolemma of body wall muscle (Kim et al., 2009).
source: C. elegans genetic studies identified genes that control the localization of SLO-1 channels in both muscles and neurons: The dystrophin complex localizes SLO-1 channels near calcium channels in the sarcolemma of body wall muscle (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2009.

claim: Alpha-catulin and dystrobrevin hierarchically organize BK channels near calcium channels at presynaptic terminals (Abraham et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2015).
source: It was also shown that alpha-catulin and dystrobrevin hierarchically organize BK channels near calcium channels at presynaptic terminals (Abraham et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abraham et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2015.

claim: Most plasma membrane proteins are packaged in cargo vesicles that exit from the ER through the COPII-dependent mechanism (Zanetti et al., 2012).
source: Once completely folded and assembled, most plasma membrane proteins are packaged in cargo vesicles that exit from the ER through the COPII-dependent mechanism (Zanetti et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanetti et al., 2012.

claim: Proteins with multiple transmembrane domains require ER membrane chaperons and cargo adaptor proteins for their efficient exit from the ER.
source: It appears that proteins with multiple transmembrane domains require ER membrane chaperons and cargo adaptor proteins for their efficient exit from the ER.
evidence: Supported by the example of yeast Erv14 in the following sentence.

claim: Yeast Erv14 is a cargo receptor that links many client membrane proteins to the COPII coat adaptor and is required for the efficient trafficking of many polytopic membrane proteins (Herzig et al., 2012).
source: For example, yeast Erv14 is a cargo receptor that links many client membrane proteins to the COPII coat adaptor and is required for the efficient trafficking of many polytopic membrane proteins (Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herzig et al., 2012.

claim: The cim16 mutation suppresses the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants.
source: Compared to slo-1(ky399gf), cim16; slo-1(ky399gf) double mutants showed improved movement (Figure 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by speed measurements in Figure 1A.

claim: The speed of cim16 mutants is comparable to that of wild-type animals.
source: Importantly, the speed of cim16 mutants was comparable to that of wild-type animals, indicating that the improved locomotory speed of the cim16;slo-1(ky399gf) double mutant is not the result of an overly active locomotory phenotype of cim16.
evidence: Stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A data.

claim: The cim16 mutation is in the erg-28 gene.
source: By a combination of SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism)-based genetic mapping and transformation rescue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we identified the cim16 mutation in erg-28 gene.
evidence: Identified through genetic mapping and rescue experiments.

claim: erg-28 is an orthologue of the yeast ergosterol biosynthesis 28 (Erg28) (Vinci et al., 2008).
source: erg-28 is an orthologue of the yeast ergosterol biosynthesis 28 (Erg28) (Vinci et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vinci et al., 2008.

claim: The ERG28 protein sequence has diverged in higher organisms (Veitia and Hurst, 2001).
source: The ERG28 protein sequence has diverged in higher organisms (Veitia and Hurst, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veitia and Hurst, 2001.

claim: Higher organism ERG28 homologues possess four predicted transmembrane domains instead of the two transmembrane domains found in yeast.
source: These homologues possess four predicted transmembrane domains instead of the two transmembrane domains found in yeast and have acquired the ER retention/retrieval motif in the C-terminus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and stated in text.

claim: Higher organism ERG28 homologues have acquired the ER retention/retrieval motif in the C-terminus.
source: These homologues possess four predicted transmembrane domains instead of the two transmembrane domains found in yeast and have acquired the ER retention/retrieval motif in the C-terminus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and stated in text.

claim: C. elegans ERG-28 shows 22.2% identity (56.4% similarity) with the human homolog C14orf1 based on a non-overlapping local alignment.
source: Although C. elegans ERG-28 retains four transmembrane domains and the ER retention/retrieval motif, it is further diverged from mammalian ERG28 proteins; it shows 22.2% identity (56.4% similarity) with the human homolog C14orf1 based on a non-overlapping local alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The erg-28(gk697770) allele has a nonsense mutation in the 33rd amino acid residue.
source: The erg-28(gk697770) allele has a nonsense mutation in the 33rd amino acid residue and the erg-28(tm6168) allele is a deletion/insertion allele that introduces a nonsense codon at 145th amino acid residue in addition to the deletion (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The erg-28(tm6168) allele is a deletion/insertion allele that introduces a nonsense codon at 145th amino acid residue.
source: The erg-28(gk697770) allele has a nonsense mutation in the 33rd amino acid residue and the erg-28(tm6168) allele is a deletion/insertion allele that introduces a nonsense codon at 145th amino acid residue in addition to the deletion (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both erg-28(gk697770) and erg-28(tm6168) alleles suppressed the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants to a level similar to cim16.
source: Both alleles also suppressed the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants to a level similar to cim16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neuronal function of slo-1 is responsible for locomotory speed (Abraham et al., 2010).
source: Our previous studies showed that neuronal function of slo-1 is responsible for locomotory speed (Abraham et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abraham et al., 2010.

claim: Neuronal, but not muscle, expression of erg-28 reverts the speed of erg-28(cim16) slo-1(ky399gf) double mutants to sluggish movement.
source: Neuronal, but not muscle, expression of erg-28, reverted the speed of erg-28(cim16) slo-1(ky399gf) double mutants to sluggish movement (Figure 1A), indicating that erg-28 functions in neurons to regulate SLO-1 function in locomotion.
evidence: Demonstrated by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: erg-28 functions in neurons to regulate SLO-1 function in locomotion.
source: Neuronal, but not muscle, expression of erg-28, reverted the speed of erg-28(cim16) slo-1(ky399gf) double mutants to sluggish movement (Figure 1A), indicating that erg-28 functions in neurons to regulate SLO-1 function in locomotion.
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Three out of four independent transgenic lines expressing human C14orf1 partially restored the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf).
source: We found that three out of four independent transgenic lines partially restored the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf), suggesting its functional conservation with C. elegans ERG-28 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: slo-1(ky399gf) mutants exhibit egg laying defects (Oh et al., 2012).
source: In addition to the sluggish locomotion, slo-1(ky399gf) mutants also exhibit egg laying defects (Oh et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Oh et al., 2012.

claim: slo-1(ky399gf) mutants exhibit loss of asymmetric gene expression in AWC olfactory neuron pairs (Troemel et al., 1999).
source: In addition to the sluggish locomotion, slo-1(ky399gf) mutants also exhibit egg laying defects (Oh et al., 2012) and loss of asymmetric gene expression in AWC olfactory neuron pairs (Troemel et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Troemel et al., 1999.

claim: erg-28 mutation partially suppresses the egg laying defect of slo-1(ky399gf).
source: erg-28 mutation was partially able to suppress the egg laying defect, as erg-28(gk697770) slo-1(ky399gf) double mutants retained less eggs than the slo-1(ky399gf) single mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Over 90% of the slo-1(ky399gf) mutant animals express the str-2 gene in both of the AWC neurons (2 AWCON).
source: Contrary to wild-type animals, over 90% of the slo-1(ky399gf) mutant animals express the str-2 gene in both of the AWC neurons (2 AWCON).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 1D data.

claim: erg-28 mutation suppresses the 2 AWCON phenotype of slo-1(ky399gf), as less than 30% of the erg-28(gk697770) slo-1(ky399gf) double mutant animals express str-2 genes in both AWC neurons.
source: erg-28 mutation was able to suppress this slo-1(ky399gf) phenotype, as less than 30% of the erg-28(gk697770) slo-1(ky399gf) double mutant animals express str-2 genes in both AWC neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The asymmetric str-2 gene expression is governed by a calcium signaling pathway involving unc-2/unc-36 voltage-gated calcium channels and downstream CaMKII, unc-43 (Alqadah et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2012).
source: The asymmetric str-2 gene expression is governed by a calcium signaling pathway involving unc-2/unc-36 voltage-gated calcium channels and downstream CaMKII, unc-43 (Alqadah et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alqadah et al., 2016; Schumacher et al., 2012.

claim: erg-28 mutation was not able to suppress the 2 AWCON phenotype of the unc-43 mutant.
source: erg-28 mutation was not able to suppress the 2 AWCON phenotype of the unc-43 mutant and minimally suppressed the unc-36 mutant (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D.

claim: erg-28 mutation minimally suppressed the 2 AWCON phenotype of the unc-36 mutant.
source: erg-28 mutation was not able to suppress the 2 AWCON phenotype of the unc-43 mutant and minimally suppressed the unc-36 mutant (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D.

claim: erg-28 is most likely to act on slo-1.
source: These results place erg-28 upstream of unc-43 and parallel to unc-2/unc-36, suggesting erg-28 is most likely to act on slo-1.
evidence: Inferred from genetic epistasis analysis with AWC differentiation pathway components.

claim: SLO-1 channels provide a negative feedback response for calcium influx and thus negatively regulate synaptic transmission.
source: Previous studies showed that SLO-1 channels provide a negative feedback response for calcium influx and thus negatively regulate synaptic transmission.
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: slo-1 loss-of-function mutants exhibit a prolonged evoked synaptic response (Abraham et al., 2010; Sancar et al., 2011).
source: Our previous study showed that slo-1 loss-of-function mutants exhibit a prolonged evoked synaptic response, whereas slo-1(ky399gf) mutants exhibit a reduced evoked synaptic response (Abraham et al., 2010; Sancar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abraham et al., 2010; Sancar et al., 2011.

claim: slo-1(ky399gf) mutants exhibit a reduced evoked synaptic response (Abraham et al., 2010; Sancar et al., 2011).
source: Our previous study showed that slo-1 loss-of-function mutants exhibit a prolonged evoked synaptic response, whereas slo-1(ky399gf) mutants exhibit a reduced evoked synaptic response (Abraham et al., 2010; Sancar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abraham et al., 2010; Sancar et al., 2011.

claim: Mutant animals with decreased levels of cholinergic synaptic transmission are resistant to aldicarb-mediated paralysis (Mahoney et al., 2006).
source: While mutant animals with decreased levels of cholinergic synaptic transmission are resistant to aldicarb-mediated paralysis, mutants with increased levels of synaptic transmission are hypersensitive to aldicarb (Mahoney et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahoney et al., 2006.

claim: Mutants with increased levels of synaptic transmission are hypersensitive to aldicarb (Mahoney et al., 2006).
source: While mutant animals with decreased levels of cholinergic synaptic transmission are resistant to aldicarb-mediated paralysis, mutants with increased levels of synaptic transmission are hypersensitive to aldicarb (Mahoney et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahoney et al., 2006.

claim: erg-28(gk697770) animals are hypersensitive to aldicarb.
source: We found that erg-28(gk697770) animals are hypersensitive to aldicarb.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A.

claim: erg-28 mutation suppresses the aldicarb-resistant phenotype of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants.
source: Furthermore, erg-28 mutation suppresses the aldicarb-resistant phenotype of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A.

claim: erg-28 mutation did not result in a higher evoked response compared to wild-type animals.
source: We did not observe a higher evoked response in erg-28 relative to wild-type animals, whereas slo-1(ky399gf) animals showed a reduced evoked response and faster decay kinetics compared to wild-type and erg-28 animals (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: slo-1(ky399gf) animals showed a reduced evoked response and faster decay kinetics compared to wild-type and erg-28 animals.
source: We did not observe a higher evoked response in erg-28 relative to wild-type animals, whereas slo-1(ky399gf) animals showed a reduced evoked response and faster decay kinetics compared to wild-type and erg-28 animals (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: erg-28 mutation significantly improved the reduced evoked response of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants, but not decay kinetics.
source: erg-28 mutation significantly improved the reduced evoked response of slo-1(ky399gf) mutants, but not decay kinetics (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: The erg-28 gene forms an operon with C14C10.5, which encodes a homolog of proteasome activator subunit 4 (PSME4).
source: The erg-28 gene forms an operon with C14C10.5, which encodes a homolog of proteasome activator subunit 4 (PSME4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of erg-28 was found in many different tissues, including muscles, intestine, and neurons.
source: The expression of erg-28 was found in many different tissues, including muscles, intestine, and neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A using promoter-GFP fusion.

claim: Promoters of operons are often promiscuous and expression of individual genes in the operons is controlled at a post-transcriptional level (Blumenthal, 2005; Blumenthal et al., 2015).
source: Promoters of operons are often promiscuous and expression of individual genes in the operons is controlled at a post-transcriptional level (Blumenthal, 2005; Blumenthal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blumenthal, 2005; Blumenthal et al., 2015.

claim: ERG-28 expression is observed mainly in neurons and muscles.
source: In this transgenic line, ERG-28 expression is observed mainly in neurons and muscles, where SLO-1 is predominantly expressed (Figure 3B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B using mCherry-tagged ERG-28.

claim: ERG-28 is abundantly expressed proximal to neuronal nuclei and localized as distinct puncta throughout the synaptic terminals and dendrites.
source: We found that ERG-28 is abundantly expressed proximal to neuronal nuclei and localized as distinct puncta throughout the synaptic terminals and dendrites (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ERG-28 puncta co-localize well with the ER marker (mCherry::PISY-1).
source: ERG-28 puncta co-localize well with the ER marker (mCherry::PISY-1) and exhibit minimal co-localization with the Golgi marker (AMAN-2::mCherry) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ERG-28 exhibits minimal co-localization with the Golgi marker (AMAN-2::mCherry).
source: ERG-28 puncta co-localize well with the ER marker (mCherry::PISY-1) and exhibit minimal co-localization with the Golgi marker (AMAN-2::mCherry) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ER extends to axonal and dendritic neural processes in C. elegans (Brockie et al., 2013; Rolls et al., 2002).
source: These results are consistent with previous studies that the ER extends to axonal and dendritic neural processes in C. elegans (Brockie et al., 2013; Rolls et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brockie et al., 2013; Rolls et al., 2002.

claim: The distribution of ERG-28 is not restricted to axon or dendrites.
source: Importantly, the distribution of ERG-28 is not restricted to axon or dendrites, indicating that ERG-28 does not have axon-dendrite polarity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of ERG-28 in both axons and dendrites.

claim: The C. elegans ERG-28 C-terminus has a well-established consensus ER retrieval/retention motif (KKXX-COOH), which interacts with coat protein complex I (COPI) (Jackson, 2014).
source: Like mammalian ERG28, the C. elegans ERG-28 C-terminus has a well-established consensus ER retrieval/retention motif (KKXX-COOH), which interacts with coat protein complex I (COPI) that mediates retrograde transport of target proteins from the cis-end of the Golgi complex to the ER, thereby ensuring the ER localization of the target proteins (Jackson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jackson, 2014.

claim: COPI mediates retrograde transport of target proteins from the cis-end of the Golgi complex to the ER (Jackson, 2014).
source: Like mammalian ERG28, the C. elegans ERG-28 C-terminus has a well-established consensus ER retrieval/retention motif (KKXX-COOH), which interacts with coat protein complex I (COPI) that mediates retrograde transport of target proteins from the cis-end of the Golgi complex to the ER, thereby ensuring the ER localization of the target proteins (Jackson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jackson, 2014.

claim: When GFP-tagged erg-28Δ7 lacking 7 amino acids at the C terminus was expressed in the DA and DB motor neurons, the overall expression was significantly decreased and normal punctate structures were no longer visible.
source: When GFP-tagged erg-28Δ7 lacking 7 amino acids at the C terminus as in cim16 allele was expressed in the DA and DB motor neurons, the overall expression was significantly decreased and normal punctate structures were no longer visible (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Some of the ERG-28 puncta are mobile.
source: Indeed, we find that some of the ERG-28 puncta are mobile (Video 1).
evidence: Shown in Video 1.

claim: ERG-28 is localized to the ER membrane through COPI interaction.
source: These observations suggest that ERG-28 is localized to the ER membrane through COPI interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of COPI binding motif and mobility of ERG-28 puncta.

claim: GFP-tagged ERG-28 co-localizes with mCherry-tagged PISY-1 from the muscle interior (muscle belly) to the muscle plasma membrane.
source: GFP-tagged ERG-28 well co-localizes with mCherry-tagged PISY-1 from the muscle interior (muscle belly) to the muscle plasma membrane (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: mCherry-tagged AMAN-2 shows a completely different pattern from that of mCherry-tagged PISY-1 and does not co-localize with GFP-tagged ERG-28.
source: By contrast, mCherry-tagged AMAN-2 shows a completely different pattern from that of mCherry-tagged PISY-1 and does not co-localize with GFP-tagged ERG-28 (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERG-28 localizes to the ER.
source: These results together indicate that ERG-28 localizes to the ER.
evidence: Concluded from co-localization experiments with ER and Golgi markers.

claim: Yeast ERG28 is a gene necessary for ergosterol (a cholesterol derivative) biosynthesis (Mo and Bard, 2005; Mo et al., 2004).
source: Yeast ERG28 is a gene necessary for ergosterol (a cholesterol derivative) biosynthesis (Mo and Bard, 2005; Mo et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mo and Bard, 2005; Mo et al., 2004.

claim: Yeast ERG28 functions as a molecular scaffold for sterol biosynthetic enzymes in ER membranes.
source: Yeast ERG28 is a gene necessary for ergosterol (a cholesterol derivative) biosynthesis (Mo and Bard, 2005; Mo et al., 2004) and functions as a molecular scaffold for sterol biosynthetic enzymes in ER membranes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mo and Bard, 2005; Mo et al., 2004.

claim: Nematodes (C. elegans) and arthropods (Drosophila) cannot synthesize sterol de novo because of the lack of key biosynthetic enzymes.
source: Nematodes (C. elegans) and arthropods (Drosophila) cannot synthesize sterol de novo because of the lack of key biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: Established knowledge about C. elegans and Drosophila sterol metabolism.

claim: None of the tested mutations in candidate biosynthetic genes (erg-24 (tm3499), erg-26 (tm1941), erg-6 (tm1781)) suppressed the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf).
source: We found that unlike erg-28, none of the tested mutations in these candidate biosynthetic genes (erg-24 (tm3499), erg-26 (tm1941), erg-6 (tm1781)) suppressed the sluggish movement of slo-1(ky399gf) (Data not shown)
evidence: Stated in text based on experimental data.

claim: The edited line, cim105[slo-1::GFP], does not show any obvious behavioral phenotypes found in slo-1 loss-of-function mutants.
source: The edited line, cim105[slo-1::GFP], designed to tag all of 12 SLO-1 isoforms (Johnson et al., 2011), does not show any obvious behavioral phenotypes found in slo-1 loss-of-function mutants, such as exaggerated head bending during forward movement, and its locomotory speed was also comparable to that of the wild type animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C)
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: GFP fusion to the C-terminus of SLO-1 in cim105 animals does not perturb in vivo SLO-1 function.
source: The edited line, cim105[slo-1::GFP], designed to tag all of 12 SLO-1 isoforms (Johnson et al., 2011), does not show any obvious behavioral phenotypes found in slo-1 loss-of-function mutants, such as exaggerated head bending during forward movement, and its locomotory speed was also comparable to that of the wild type animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), indicating that GFP fusion to the C-terminus of SLO-1 in cim105 animals does not perturb in vivo SLO-1 function.
evidence: Inferred from normal behavioral phenotypes of cim105 animals.

claim: SLO-1 channels are mainly observed in neurons and muscles as discrete puncta.
source: While weak, diffused SLO-1 channels can be detected in the nerve ring, SLO-1 channels are mainly observed in neurons and muscles as discrete puncta (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SLO-1::GFP expression was drastically reduced in erg-28 mutant animals both in the nerve ring and muscles.
source: When we compared SLO-1::GFP expression in wild-type, erg-28 (gk697770), and erg-28(cim16) mutant animals by taking advantage of cim105[slo-1::GFP], SLO-1::GFP expression was drastically reduced in erg-28 mutant animals both in the nerve ring and muscles, although not completely abolished (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The total amount of SLO-1 was reduced in erg-28 mutants.
source: When measured by western analysis using whole animals, the total amount of SLO-1 was reduced in erg-28 mutants, confirming the overall reduction of SLO-1 amount (Figure 5D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D by western blot.

claim: The expression of mCherry-tagged ERG-28 restored the SLO-1::GFP expression to a level comparable to the heterozygotic expression of SLO-1::GFP in both neurons and muscles.
source: The expression of mCherry-tagged ERG-28 restored the SLO-1::GFP expression to a level comparable to the heterozygotic expression of SLO-1::GFP (one copy of untagged SLO-1 and one copy of GFP-tagged SLO-1) in both neurons and muscles (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: SLO-1::GFP and ELKS-1::fRFP are well co-localized although some SLO-1::GFP puncta did not co-localize with ELKS-1::fRFP, and vice versa.
source: We find that SLO-1::GFP and ELKS-1::fRFP are well co-localized although we occasionally observed that some SLO-1::GFP puncta that did not co-localize with ELKS-1::fRFP, and vice versa (Figure 4D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the erg-28 mutant, the SLO-1 puncta were co-localized with ELKS-1::fRFP.
source: In the erg-28 mutant, the SLO-1 puncta were co-localized with ELKS-1::fRFP (Figure 4E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ERG-28 is required for the normal level of SLO-1 expression in muscles and neurons, but not for the localization at either presynaptic terminals or dense bodies in muscles.
source: These results indicate that ERG-28 is required for the normal level of SLO-1 expression in muscles and neurons, but not for the localization at either presynaptic terminals or dense bodies in muscles.
evidence: Concluded from co-localization experiments showing reduced but correctly localized SLO-1 in erg-28 mutants.

claim: SLO-1::GFP puncta rarely co-localize with mCherry::ERG-28 puncta although potential co-localization can be occasionally observed in neuronal cell bodies.
source: Indeed, we find that SLO-1::GFP puncta rarely co-localize with mCherry::ERG-28 puncta although potential co-localization can be occasionally observed in neuronal cell bodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERG-28 is most likely to function in ER for the efficient trafficking of SLO-1 to the plasma membrane.
source: Taken together, ERG-28 is most likely to function in ER for the efficient trafficking of SLO-1 to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from ER localization of ERG-28 and reduced SLO-1 at plasma membrane in erg-28 mutants.

claim: When erg-28 mutant animals were grown in the presence of bortezomib, SLO-1 expression at presynaptic terminals was increased by 50%.
source: When erg-28 mutant animals were grown in the presence of bortezomib, SLO-1 expression at presynaptic terminals, but not in cell bodies, was increased by 50%, while the wild type animals showed no statistically significant change (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ERG-28 protects SLO-1 from degradation in the ER and is not an obligatory factor for SLO-1 exit from the ER.
source: This suggests that ERG-28 protects SLO-1 from degradation in the ER and is not an obligatory factor for SLO-1 exit from the ER.
evidence: Inferred from proteasome inhibitor experiments showing partial restoration of SLO-1.

claim: The lower expression level of SLO-1 at the plasma membrane in erg-28 mutant is at least in part due to proteasomal degradation.
source: Thus, the lower expression level of SLO-1 at the plasma membrane in erg-28 mutant is at least in part due to proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Concluded from bortezomib treatment experiments.

claim: ddi-1 is an orthologue of yeast and human DDI1, which is thought to be a shuttling factor that delivers ubiquitinated substrates to proteasomes (Gabriely et al., 2008).
source: ddi-1 is an orthologue of yeast and human DDI1, which is thought to be a shuttling factor that delivers ubiquitinated substrates to proteasomes (Gabriely et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gabriely et al., 2008.

claim: In yeast, DDI-1 appears to act as a negative regulator for general exocytosis (White et al., 2011).
source: In yeast, DDI-1 appears to act as a negative regulator for general exocytosis (White et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2011.

claim: The ddi-1(ok1468) single mutant did not show any significant difference in SLO-1 expression level in neurons and muscles compared to wild type.
source: Compared to wild type, the ddi-1(ok1468) single mutant did not show any significant difference in SLO-1 expression level in neurons and muscles.
evidence: Stated in text and supported by Figure 5B-D.

claim: ddi-1(ok1468);erg-28(gk697770) double mutants showed a significantly higher expression of SLO-1 at the plasma membrane than the erg-28(gk697770) single mutant.
source: However, ddi-1(ok1468);erg-28(gk697770) double mutants showed a significantly higher expression of SLO-1 at the plasma membrane than the erg-28(gk697770) single mutant, albeit to a lesser extent than wild-type animals (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: ERG-28 promotes SLO-1 channel trafficking to the plasma membrane by shielding SLO-1 channels from proteasomal degradation.
source: Taken together, we conclude that ERG-28 promotes SLO-1 channel trafficking to the plasma membrane by shielding SLO-1 channels from proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Concluded from proteasome inhibitor and ddi-1 experiments.

claim: SLO-1 BK channels are a central mediator of alcohol intoxication (Davies et al., 2003; Davis et al., 2014; Dopico et al., 1996).
source: Previous studies have shown that SLO-1 BK channels are a central mediator of alcohol intoxication (Davies et al., 2003; Davis et al., 2014; Dopico et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 2003; Davis et al., 2014; Dopico et al., 1996.

claim: erg-28 mutants exhibit significant ethanol-resistant locomotory behavior, albeit to a lower degree than slo-1 loss-of-function mutants.
source: erg-28 mutants exhibit significant ethanol-resistant locomotory behavior, albeit to a lower degree than slo-1 loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is a quantitative correlation between the degree of alcohol sensitivity and the amount of SLO-1 expression at presynaptic terminals.
source: erg-28 mutants exhibit significant ethanol-resistant locomotory behavior, albeit to a lower degree than slo-1 loss-of-function mutants. This suggests that there is a quantitative correlation between the degree of alcohol sensitivity and the amount of SLO-1 expression at presynaptic terminals.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that erg-28 mutants with reduced SLO-1 show intermediate alcohol resistance.

claim: The alcohol sensitivity of the ddi-1 mutant was not different from the wild type.
source: While the alcohol sensitivity of the ddi-1 mutant was not different from the wild type, ddi-1;erg-28 double mutants were more sensitive than erg-28 single mutants.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ddi-1;erg-28 double mutants were more sensitive to alcohol than erg-28 single mutants.
source: While the alcohol sensitivity of the ddi-1 mutant was not different from the wild type, ddi-1;erg-28 double mutants were more sensitive than erg-28 single mutants.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The increased SLO-1 channels in the ddi-1;erg-28 double mutant are functional.
source: Thus, the increased SLO-1 channels in the ddi-1;erg-28 double mutant are functional and 50% of SLO-1 is sufficient for normal alcohol sensitivity (Figure 6, Videos 2–4).
evidence: Inferred from the restoration of alcohol sensitivity in ddi-1;erg-28 double mutants.

claim: 50% of SLO-1 is sufficient for normal alcohol sensitivity.
source: Thus, the increased SLO-1 channels in the ddi-1;erg-28 double mutant are functional and 50% of SLO-1 is sufficient for normal alcohol sensitivity (Figure 6, Videos 2–4).
evidence: Inferred from ddi-1;erg-28 double mutant showing normal alcohol sensitivity with ~50% SLO-1 levels.

claim: The density of BK channels at presynaptic terminals influences synaptic transmission and neuronal function.
source: Our study demonstrates that the density of BK channels at presynaptic terminals influences synaptic transmission and neuronal function
evidence: Demonstrated by the effects of reduced SLO-1 levels in erg-28 mutants on synaptic transmission and behavior.

claim: ERG28 was originally identified in yeast as a scaffold in the ER to tether a group of ergosterol synthesizing enzymes, which form a sterol C4 demethylase complex.
source: ERG28 was originally identified in yeast as a scaffold in the ER to tether a group of ergosterol synthesizing enzymes, which form a sterol C4 demethylase complex.
evidence: Established knowledge about yeast ERG28 function.

claim: Mutation in Arabidopsis ERG28 results in accumulation of cryptic sterol biosynthetic intermediates and consequent inhibition of polar auxin transport.
source: Instead, mutation in ERG28 results in accumulation of cryptic sterol biosynthetic intermediates and consequent inhibition of polar auxin transport.
evidence: Stated in text referring to Arabidopsis study.

claim: C. elegans obtains the final sterol products from plants or mammals, such as ergosterol, sitosterol, and cholesterol.
source: C. elegans is not able to synthesize cholesterol de novo, and thus obtains the final sterol products from plants or mammals, such as ergosterol, sitosterol, and cholesterol.
evidence: Established knowledge about C. elegans sterol metabolism.

claim: Substitution of cholesterol with lanosterol does not allow C. elegans growth (Lee et al., 2005).
source: Substitution of cholesterol with lanosterol, which is a precursor of cholesterol that has a C4 methyl group, does not allow C. elegans growth (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2005.

claim: C. elegans does not possess biologically active known cholesterol C4 methyl derivatives (Mahanti et al., 2014).
source: Furthermore, C. elegans does not possess biologically active known cholesterol C4 methyl derivatives (Mahanti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mahanti et al., 2014.

claim: It is reported that hERG28 interacts with CLN8, an ER-resident membrane protein involved in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Passantino et al., 2013).
source: For instance, it is reported that hERG28 interacts with CLN8, an ER-resident membrane protein involved in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Passantino et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Passantino et al., 2013.

claim: CLN8 mutation in humans causes altered levels of sphingolipid and phospholipid.
source: CLN8 mutation in humans causes altered levels of sphingolipid and phospholipid.
evidence: Stated in text as established knowledge.

claim: In the absence of ERG-28, functional SLO-1 channels can still be transported to the plasma membrane.
source: This suggests that in the absence of ERG-28 in the ER, functional SLO-1 channels can still be transported to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from proteasome inhibitor experiments showing partial restoration of SLO-1.

claim: ERG-28 is not an obligatory factor necessary for the ER exit of SLO-1.
source: Also, in the absence of ERG-28, SLO-1 does not appear to accumulate in cell bodies. Thus, ERG-28 is not an obligatory factor necessary for the ER exit of SLO-1.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of SLO-1 accumulation in cell bodies in erg-28 mutants.

claim: The SLO-1 channel consists of four pore-forming α subunits and auxiliary subunits.
source: The SLO-1 channel consists of four pore-forming α subunits and auxiliary subunits, and may require a molecular chaperone that aids channel folding and assembly.
evidence: Established knowledge about BK channel structure.

claim: ERG-28 acts as a chaperone for SLO-1 channel folding/assembly intermediates so that they are not prematurely recognized as misfolded proteins and targeted for degradation.
source: Our data support the model in which ERG-28 acts as a chaperone for SLO-1 channel folding/assembly intermediates so that they are not prematurely recognized as misfolded proteins and targeted for degradation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data showing ERG-28 protects SLO-1 from degradation.

claim: RIC-3 promotes nicotinic acetylcholine receptor surface expression (Halevi et al., 2002).
source: Designated ER proteins for specific ion channel folding/assembly and trafficking are common, and include RIC-3 that promotes nicotinic acetylcholine receptor surface expression (Halevi et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Halevi et al., 2002.

claim: CALF-1 facilitates synaptic localization of UNC-2 voltage-gated calcium channels (Saheki and Bargmann, 2009).
source: Designated ER proteins for specific ion channel folding/assembly and trafficking are common, and include RIC-3 that promotes nicotinic acetylcholine receptor surface expression (Halevi et al., 2002), CALF-1 that facilitates synaptic localization of UNC-2 voltage-gated calcium channels (Saheki and Bargmann, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Saheki and Bargmann, 2009.

claim: NLF-1 regulates axonal localization of NALC channels (Xie et al., 2013).
source: Designated ER proteins for specific ion channel folding/assembly and trafficking are common, and include RIC-3 that promotes nicotinic acetylcholine receptor surface expression (Halevi et al., 2002), CALF-1 that facilitates synaptic localization of UNC-2 voltage-gated calcium channels (Saheki and Bargmann, 2009), and NLF-1 that regulates axonal localization of NALC channels (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2013.

claim: ERG-28 is equally distributed to the dendrites and axons.
source: For example, ERG-28 is equally distributed to the dendrites and axons (Figure 3C), whereas SLO-1 is relatively specific to axons, suggesting its involvement in the trafficking of dendritic membrane proteins.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SLO-1 is relatively specific to axons.
source: For example, ERG-28 is equally distributed to the dendrites and axons (Figure 3C), whereas SLO-1 is relatively specific to axons, suggesting its involvement in the trafficking of dendritic membrane proteins.
evidence: Stated in text based on known SLO-1 localization.

claim: ERG-28 may be involved in the trafficking of dendritic membrane proteins.
source: For example, ERG-28 is equally distributed to the dendrites and axons (Figure 3C), whereas SLO-1 is relatively specific to axons, suggesting its involvement in the trafficking of dendritic membrane proteins.
evidence: Inferred from ERG-28's presence in dendrites where SLO-1 is not predominantly localized.

claim: The aspartyl proteinase domain of the yeast DDI1 is important for its function as a negative regulator of general secretion.
source: The aspartyl proteinase domain of the yeast DDI1 is important for its function as a negative regulator of general secretion.
evidence: Stated in text based on yeast studies.

claim: The aspartyl proteinase activity of DDI-1 is required for the activation of the ER-associated SKN-1 isoform during proteasomal dysfunction in C. elegans (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
source: Recently, the aspartyl proteinase activity of DDI-1 was shown to be required for the activation of the ER-associated SKN-1 isoform during proteasomal dysfunction in C. elegans (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016.

claim: Functional alcohol tolerance has a correlation with BK channel levels at the plasma membrane (Palacio et al., 2015; Pietrzykowski et al., 2008).
source: Previous studies indicated that functional alcohol tolerance has a correlation with BK channel levels at the plasma membrane, although the mechanisms by which its levels are controlled appear to involve several distinct steps (Palacio et al., 2015; Pietrzykowski et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Palacio et al., 2015; Pietrzykowski et al., 2008.

claim: SLO-1 levels are controlled by ERG-28/DDI-1 in the ER.
source: Given that our current study shows that SLO-1 levels are controlled by ERG-28/DDI-1 in the ER, it is tempting to speculate that ERG-28/DDI-1 adjusts overall SLO-1 levels depending on cellular stress or physiological necessity.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental data showing ERG-28 and DDI-1 regulate SLO-1 degradation.

claim: ERG-28/DDI-1 may adjust overall SLO-1 levels depending on cellular stress or physiological necessity.
source: Given that our current study shows that SLO-1 levels are controlled by ERG-28/DDI-1 in the ER, it is tempting to speculate that ERG-28/DDI-1 adjusts overall SLO-1 levels depending on cellular stress or physiological necessity.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the findings.
